 LIFESTYLE Personal Finance Can you just walk into a Social Security office without an appointment? These are the few cases when you can do it
 Although the Social Security Administration encourages people to book appointments before visiting a local office, certain circumstances can qualify for same-day assistance, including urgent cases and people facing particular barriers
 Social Security Administration 
 EUAN BURNS (SAM)

 Visiting a Social Security office without an appointment does not automatically mean you will be refused help.
 While the Social Security Administration (SSA) has encouraged appointment-based services to manage demand and reduce waiting times, its guidance also recognizes that some people need assistance without being able to arrange a visit in advance.
 Social Security: When is COLA announced, how is it determined and how much can people expect? M.C. The agency introduced a nationwide appointment-focused approach on January 6, 2025. The original announcement explained that appointments would be required for in-person services, including applications for Social Security cards.
 However, it also made clear that people who could not arrange an appointment, or did not want one, would not simply be turned away.
 The SSA specifically identified vulnerable individuals, military personnel, people with terminal illnesses and those requiring immediate or specialized attention as examples of people who could still walk into an office.
 Importantly, the agency's subsequent internal instructions provided further detail about when staff should consider helping walk-in visitors on the same day.
 Those instructions were made obsolete in April 2026, with the accompanying explanation saying the agency wanted to move away from an appointment-focused policy and allow offices to provide more same-day service.
 That makes it important to distinguish between being allowed to request assistance without an appointment and having a guaranteed right to immediate service. Local office circumstances and the urgency of the case can still affect what happens when someone arrives.
 Which situations can qualify for walk-in assistance?
 The SSA's previous detailed guidance provides useful examples of circumstances in which same-day attention may be appropriate. These include:
 People facing an urgent financial situation: Individuals experiencing dire need may require immediate help, particularly when a delay could have serious consequences.
 People with terminal illnesses: The agency recognizes that individuals facing serious health circumstances may need more immediate or specialized attention.
 Military personnel: Members of the military are specifically included among the groups that may receive walk-in assistance.
 Vulnerable individuals facing barriers: People who struggle to access appointments or navigate the usual service channels may qualify for additional consideration.
 Special Social Security number cases: Certain situations involving identity, employment verification, harassment, abuse or threats to personal safety can require more urgent handling.
 Time-sensitive benefit cases: Issues involving immediate payments, critical pending claims or corrections to death records may also justify same-day attention.
 The guidance additionally gives local office managers discretion to decide when an in-person visit should be handled immediately. Shorter transactions, known as Express Interviews, can also be completed at the first point of contact when appropriate.
 Examples include benefit verification, submitting evidence, changing direct deposit details, requesting a 1099 form and updating an address.
 However, these examples should not be interpreted as a guarantee that every visitor in one of these categories will automatically receive immediate service. The circumstances of the case and the office's ability to provide assistance matter.
 How to arrange an appointment before visiting
 For routine matters, booking ahead remains the safest approach. The SSA's online appointment service allows visitors to answer questions about the assistance they need and determine whether their issue can be handled online or requires a phone or in-person appointment.
 People can also call the national Social Security number at 1-800-772-1213, Monday through Friday, from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. in most U.S. time zones. Those who are deaf or hard of hearing can use the TTY number, 1-800-325-0778.
 There are also reasons to consider completing business online instead. A personal my Social Security account allows users to access benefit information, check application progress, manage certain details and request replacement documents without travelling to an office.
 The SSA's September 2026 performance figures showed that customers with appointments waited an average of approximately six minutes in field offices, compared with a longer average for visitors without appointments. Actual waiting times vary between locations.
 Ultimately, walking into a Social Security office without an appointment can still be an option, particularly when a situation is urgent or requires specialized attention.
 But anyone planning a routine visit should check the local office's arrangements and try to schedule ahead to avoid an unnecessary journey or lengthy wait.
